title: Copycat Tech: Why the AI Bubble Might Burst
content:
Large language models share an open secret: they’re trained on the same data and generally detect the same patterns. Engineers race to produce updated versions only for their competitors to catch up to them within a few weeks. This makes for high production costs but low switching costs for customers.

It also makes for a fragile business model. 

This logic explains why many fear a bubble. A site called isaiprofitable.com adds up major AI companies’ announced revenue and subtracts expenditure — and comes up with a large negative number. AI companies have excited us with promises of revenue, overlooking whether those exceed the cost of producing them. Policymakers, in Europe and elsewhere, should be wary of pouring public money into gigafactories or other schemes to build copycat large language models just as investors are beginning to question the likelihood of them making profits. 

When ChatGPT 3.5 came out, OpenAI’s strategy looked like a classic three-stage capital expenditure play:

  • Build up a monopoly too expensive to replicate. 
  • Raise prices. 
  • Profit.

title: Armenia’s Relations With Russia? Worsening
content:
If you want one example of Armenia’s problems in shaking itself free of Russia’s influence, look at its rail system. Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan has repeatedly called for Russia to show flexibility and potentially transfer the concession to a third country acceptable to both sides. On 24 August, he again urged Russia to sell its concession rights to a mutually acceptable third party.

Russia has not answered, and it is unlikely to accept the idea. It has been running an escalating campaign to make life hard for Pashinyan, who was reelected in June. Putin makes no secret of this; indeed, he seems to delight in the (considerable) influence he can bring to bear.

That was clear at the September 1 meeting between the Russian and Armenian leaders at Bishkek, on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit. The reason is Armenia’s pursuit of closer ties with the European Union.

Putin sees this as a threat, as he once did with Ukraine. The EU’s anti-corruption, free trade, liberal democratic ethos is the antithesis of Russia’s approach.

title: CEPA Podcast: General (Ret.) Daniel Petrescu on What is Next for the NATO Alliance
content:
The CEPA Podcast is a series of dynamic interviews, bringing together leaders and experts from both sides of the Atlantic to explore the most important challenges shaping our world today. 

In this episode, General (Ret.) Daniel Petrescu, Romania’s former Chief of the Defence Staff, joins to explore where NATO goes after this year’s summit in Ankara. Drawing on Romania’s experience intercepting Russian drones out of its own airspace, he argues the alliance’s real potential lies in how fast allies can field and integrate new capabilities to face today’s threats. Petrescu makes the case for how a stronger Romania can bolster the alliance and why the Black Sea deserves more attention as a region for NATO’s leadership. 

Speakers:  

  • Gen. (Ret.) Daniel Petrescu, Member, International Leadership Council, Center for European Policy Analysis; Chief of the Defence Staff, Romanian Armed Forces (2019-2023) 

    • Moderated by: 

  • Kari Odermann, Fellow, Center for European Policy Analysis 

    • Listen and subscribe on Spotify, Apple Podcasts, Google Podcasts, and wherever you get your podcasts. 

    Click here to listen now. For questions regarding this episode, please contact Press@cepa.org

title: Dangerous Partners: The Russia-China Military Embrace
content:
Moscow and Beijing have not built a joint military space command, and they do not need one. Selective cooperation in missile warning, navigation, air and missile defense, and potentially counterspace operations is already making both countries harder to deter and US space power more vulnerable.

There is no evidence of a combined Russian-Chinese space command, no confirmed joint anti-satellite force, no integrated missile-warning network comparable to NORAD, and no known arrangement under which an attack on one country’s space assets would oblige the other to respond. Yet Moscow and Beijing are increasingly cooperating precisely in areas where limited coordination can produce disproportionate strategic effects.

Their relationship is best understood not as an emerging military alliance, but as selective strategic integration. Using this approach, they increasingly exchange technology, operational experience, infrastructure, and strategic concepts designed to reduce US military advantages.

Their joint exercises have so far displayed limited interoperability, but even modest coordination can complicate US and NATO defense planning.

title: NATO Must Match Russia’s Long-Range Missile Arsenal
content:
On the sidelines of this summer’s NATO Summit in Ankara, 12 allies, led by the UK, commited $50bn to developing deep strike precision capabilities. Then, in August, the new British Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced Ukraine would be given blueprints for long-range Storm Shadow cruise missiles.

These steps were welcome, but without further action they will not fill the long-range fire gap with Russia. Many of the new capabilities planned by the European group will not be available until the next decade.

European NATO not only lacks the integrated air and missile defense equipment to counter Russia’s long-range capabilities, but don’t have enough equally powerful missiles to deter the Kremlin.

Allied states and Ukraine need to come together to develop a strategy to remove the disparity in long-range weapons, especially as the alliance confronts production and cost issues around air defense systems and shortfalls in missile deliveries.

The Kremlin has invested heavily in an array of long-range weapons systems since 2018, including the Avangard, the Iksander, and the still experimental Burevestnik, giving it a dynamic range of capabilities, some of which are hypersonic.

title: AI’s Rubberstamp
content:
It’s the latest tech challenge: identify when students, authors, and others depend on AI to produce content. Anthropic places invisible statistical watermarks in Claude-generated text. Google deploys a similar technique, SynthID, in Gemini. OpenAI is testing watermarking ChatGPT responses. 

Under Europe’s Artificial Intelligence Act, new labeling rules took effect this summer. Companies must now mark AI-generated content and deepfakes that relate to public interest topics, including politics, public health, security, and the economy. The only exception is for content that has undergone genuine human review or editorial control.

While the US has no federal requirement to watermark AI-generated content, Congress has considered legislation, and several states have acted. California’s AI Transparency Act requires large providers to offer detection tools and embed origin disclosures in AI-generated images, video, and audio, though not text.

title: US Courts Emerge as Tech’s Sheriff
content:
When European officials imposed antitrust fines on Silicon Valley giants, the US trade office criticized them for creating “massive uncertainty” for US exports. The House Judiciary Committee held dedicated hearings on “Anti-American Antitrust.”

But US court cases are proving more dangerous to US tech than European penalties. Meta’s decision to pay up to $17.1 billion to 47 states to settle a three-year-old lawsuit about child safety is more onerous than European fines. US courts have also imposed restrictions on Apple’s app stores and declared Google’s ad marketplace a monopoly.

How far the penalties will go remains uncertain. While the Meta settlement goes far beyond any European decisions to impose changes to a tech company’s business model, US judges have decided against any breakups for Google, and the changes to Apple’s app store remain mired in litigation.

Yet a surprising transatlantic consensus is emerging over the need to rein in tech. Both Americans and Europeans share the same concerns regarding children’s online safety and tech’s power, and US courts overall have emboldened European officials to ignore threats of trade retaliation.

title: Foreign-Built US Warships? It Might Work
content:
The United States lacks warships. A shipbuilding sector still suited to peacetime, a fast-multiplying Chinese navy, and allied yards offering impressive capabilities are aligning to provide new options for Washington.

The Trump administration has made revitalizing American shipbuilding a major policy priority, but this will take time. As the 2026 Maritime Action Plan stated: “The United States does not have the capacity necessary to scale up the domestic shipbuilding industry to the rate required to meet national priorities.”

What to do? In an August 13 presidential memorandum on Rebuilding the United States Navy and America’s Shipbuilding Industrial Base, the White House advocated what it called the “Finland Model” of allied shipbuilding to allow the first two ships in multi-ship buys to be constructed in select foreign shipyards in exchange for, or in response to, robust investment in America’s maritime industrial base.

title: Ukraine Rethinks Mine Clearance for a New Age
content:
The technology of war is evolving faster than the systems it is designed to counter. Artificial intelligence, drones, sensors, and other technologies are transforming how weapons are developed, deployed, and concealed.

The clean-up technology for mines and other explosive ordnance is not immune to these changes. Much of what organizations have learned over the decades has been made obsolete by new technologies. In Ukraine and elsewhere, a new approach is needed.

The scale of contamination is now just part of the challenge: the variety, sophistication, and concealability of explosive threats make them increasingly difficult to detect, classify, and safely neutralize.

The success or failure of Ukraine’s mine clearance will directly affect how quickly contaminated land can be returned to productive use and how successfully the country can recover, and will offer lessons for the rest of the world.

The mine problem is often framed in terms of scale: How much land is contaminated? How many munitions remain? And how much time and money will clearance require? As critical as these questions are, there is a more fundamental problem: the evolving nature of the threat.

title: No Magic Bullet to End Russian Sabotage
content:
The Kremlin is increasing sabotage operations across Europe. There have been arson attacks at drone factories, incendiary devices thrown at a producer of encryption tools for government networks, and rocket attacks on power grids. 

Among incidents that are now almost routine in Germany, Poland, and the Baltic states, Ukraine’s most consistent supporters, the attack by three drones at Leipzig airport in August – which by a miracle failed to kill or maim – stands apart as a clear escalation.

German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, blaming Russia for this sabotage attack, said: “We do not view the incident in Leipzig as an isolated case, but rather see it in the context of other hybrid actions.” He continued: “We proceed from the assumption that Germany will become a target for further hybrid attacks by Russia.”

He’s right. While his assessment offers a gloomy view of European security, it is also realistic. The continent has been deeply shaken by the brazen and worsening sabotage campaign organized by the Kremlin and its intelligence agencies since the beginning of the war in Ukraine.

title: US Chips Policy Gains In Intelligence
content:
When the US enacted the CHIPS Act four years ago, the first goal was to revitalize domestic semiconductor manufacturing. Out of the $59 billion budget, two-thirds went to grants and loan guarantees for foundries. Intel and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) built plants in Arizona. Samsung invested in Texas. Micron invested in New York.

But new CHIPS Act funding pivots away from treating success as a simple count of chip production. It funds a broad range of artificial intelligence computing capabilities: advanced packaging, interconnects, memory, photonics, materials and secure electronics.

The pivot is welcome. The US will never be entirely self-sufficient in chips. Instead, it needs to build US capability at critical bottlenecks, and avoid asking US taxpayers to finance every layer of a global supply chain. If it is to meet the challenge from China, Washington needs, above all, to work with trusted democratic allies – seeing them as assets, not as dangerous competitors.

title: The Quiet Battle Against Russia’s Shadow Fleet
content:
Ukraine’s allies have gradually persuaded flag-of-convenience states to stop providing registration for Russian ships. This quiet campaign has forced Moscow to re-flag the ships as Russian to prevent them from being seized, but that comes with a heavy financial penalty. 

A flag-of-convenience vessel can often get away with selling Russian oil in violation of sanctions at the market rate, while the false flags give service providers, buyers, and equipment suppliers plausible deniability. When ships are forced to sail under Russian colors, they cannot evade the international price cap on Russian oil, reducing the Kremlin’s income and the flow of funds for its war on Ukraine.

Flags of convenience are nothing new. Countries such as Liberia and Panama have raised revenue for decades by flagging ships with few questions asked or standards enforced. Shipping companies are attracted because they can evade safety, labor, and environmental standards, as well as sanctions

title: Europe and US Need a Plan for Economic Friendly Fire
content:
The US Senate passed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act by 86 votes to 11 on August 7. A House version was introduced three days later, and it includes a provision that deserves particular attention in Europe.

Section 113 would require the President to impose duties of up to 100% on US imports from countries that make new purchases of Russian crude oil or natural gas, rank among the five largest importers by volume, or are in the top five facilitators of sanctions evasion. An amendment to remove the tariff authority, which has a national-interest waiver, was rejected.

Russian energy revenues help finance the war against Ukraine, and Europe has spent years — and much political capital — reducing its imports. Under binding EU legislation, remaining imports under qualifying long-term Russian LNG contracts end on January 1, 2027, with qualifying long-term pipeline contracts ending nine months later, subject to a storage safeguard that could delay the latter for a further month.
